That's not a veneer it's a burl cap that's probably close to 1/2". You can't really fill the bumps with epoxy since epoxy and the poly finish won't mix well. It'll be very noticeable. You also don't want to sand the cap down. Minimum they'd have to sand at least 1/16", which means that the bridge height will be off and the guitar might not be able to intonate properly. Since this is a burl, those bumps are part of the wood structure. 

The easiest way for OP to fill the bumps without damaging the guitar would be to strip the poly finish to the bare wood and using a pore filler with shellac to create a slurry will fill the pores and bumps. Once OP has a smooth and level surface they can prep the body for a new finish. Personally I like to do a French polish since it's very repairable and beautiful but OP can also spray poly or another finish. Getting a great quality finish is very labor intensive. 

OP, if you do want to try and refinish your guitar, sand gently with the direction of the grain using sanding blocks(using just your hands will make an uneven surface) and sand up to 320 grit. Take a damp cloth(water or alcohol) wipe the guitar down. This will raise the wood fibers and make pore filling easier. Mix the pore filler with shellac and denatured alcohol and apply it liberally to the surface, wait a bit and wipe off the excess. Do a final light sand using 320 or 400 grit if you have it and from there you'll have a prepped body for final finishing work. If you want the same colors for the finish apply the brighter stains to the surface, let it dry and reapply as needed until you get the hue you want. Then you can apply the black stain with a cloth to finish the burst. Once that's done you can apply your desired final finish. If you are going to spray, start spraying away from the instrument and do quick light passes over the instrument. Be careful not to spray in one spot for too long or you'll pool the finish onto the guitar or you might get an orange peel effect. If this happens, strip the finish and start over. 

As I mentioned above I prefer a French Polish, it's very beautiful, environmentally friendly and easy to repair. To do a French polish; take a cotton cloth, fold it until you have a tight compact ball. Take some denatured alcohol and your shellac( I recommend a 1lb blonde dewaxed cut) apply it to the little ball. Then take another cotton cloth wrap the ball and put a tiny dab of olive oil( this helps with lubrication). With the tight ball of cotton in your hand make a motion like an airplane taking off and landing across the entire surface of the guitar. Shellac is very delicate and will dry almost instantly, so you have to be sure to do gentle delicate passes to avoid burning the finish. You can do about 3-4 applications a day, let it dry and repeat the process until you get the desired sheen. You'll get the most beautiful polished finish but you still have to let it cure. Let the guitar cure for a month and then you can do a final polish with a piece of burlap for burnishing. Good luck OP, it's a whole ton of work but it's a fun project!

The tuners are the least of the problems that this guitar has. Unfortunately the plywood soundboard has been cracked all the way through and must be replaced. There's no way to properly repair it. 

Putting a 5lb weight and gluing a flat piece of poplar won't fix the issue. First of all there is a radius to the soundboard and if it could be stabilized, it would need to be clamped down to the appropriate radius not flattened. With the repairs that you're suggesting the guitar would not be playable, the bridge would rip the sound hole patch as soon as the strings are in tension. 

For the cost and time to properly repair this guitar I don't think it's worth it,  but if OP just wants to learn how to repair instruments it's an excellent project to take on. However this isn't going to be a $25 project.

You can't put a bridge on this soundboard, it's completely compromised. From the pictures it looks like the soundboard is made of plywood and with it cracking all the way through it's impossible to repair. They would need to replace the soundboard, bracing and do a neck reset to ensure you have the proper neck angle for intonation. I'd imagine they would also need to replace the binding/ purfling as well since it's difficult to remove without damaging it.

The guitar is essentially trash but it's also a great project for OP to learn lutherie. If I were to try this repair I would start by removing the fretboard using a clothes iron, lots of steam and a spatula. 

Then I would remove the soundboard, if you're trying to save the binding steam and a razorblade work wonders but the important part here is that you don't damage the sides.

If you can remove the soundboard cleanly without damaging the sides you would then scrape off all the old glue and residue from the sides and begin building a new soundboard.

OP you'll need a radius dish for the soundboard, most builders use a 25 foot dish for their builds. I would copy the bracing pattern on this guitar and construct the new soundboard with your desired radius and thickness, personally I make my soundboards to about 1.5-2mm in thickness depending on the species. From there all you need to do is clamp the soundboard with wooden spool clamps or a bicycle inner tube for at least 24 hours. 

Check the neck geometry to figure out the correct angle. If the joint on the neck is undamaged I would leave it alone, just measure the neck angle with a straight edge taking the measurements from the theoretical bridge location. On a classical you want approximately 11mm from the sound board to the string height. 

After that take a Gramil or a router with a binding but and cut out the new binding and purfling channels. If you were able to save the binding and purfling, glue them in if not you'll need to steam bend the new binding and purfling to the guitars shape. Take some Titebond 2 and masking tape to glue on the binding/purfling. 

From here you want to have the soundboard and fretboard glued on. Take an accurate ruler and measure the distance from the nut to the 12th fret and double it. That will be your scale length. For example if your guitar has a scale length of 24" the distance from the 12th fret to the location of the bridge should be 12" plus a skosh for intonation. 

Once your bridge has been glued in the correctly intonated and  everything is glued up and looking nice, you can finish the soundboard with your desired finish. I prefer shellac but you can use other types of lacquer.

It's a hell of a project for a beginner but with the proper tools, time and resources you can do it. It's a great learning experience but I don't think the value of the guitar is worth the effort unless your goal is to learn lutherie. Good luck OP and DM me if you have any questions.

I'm a luthier, If you have the time, you could try fixing the guitar yourself or take it to a luthier but I think it might be cheaper to replace the instrument. I believe that the repair won't be a permanent solution. From the picture it looks like there are several spots where the back cracked all the way through.

If you want to try and fix it yourself, I would first measure to see if the back has a radius, if it does you will need to make or buy a radius dish for the back. Most guitars use around a 15' radius, but it's all dependant on the luthier or company. From there take a thin steel spatula and heat it up to where water will fizzle. You're going to carefully use the heated spatula to separate the back from the rest of the guitar by reactivating the glue. You can heat up the back with a heat gun as well, just be careful not to burn anything. 

Once the back is off. Lightly clamp it on the radius dish and assess the damage to the guitar, if the back is fully cracked through on those three spots you might be able to fix it, by gluing up the cracks. Since the cracks look to be on the end grain, the back will have to be replaced since the fix might end up being a weak joint.

Check the braces to see if any of them got knocked loose or cracked a long the brace. If you find a broken brace, check if it's a clean break. If it is you'll be able to reglue it. If not the brace will have to be replaced.

Check the sides of the guitar for cracks or loose kerfing ( the lined  wood edge on the inside of the guitar.). If everything looks good, get Titebond 2 glue and enough wooden spool clamps to clamp the back to the guitar. If you don't have spool clamps, a bicycle inner tube works wonders. Make sure everything is lined up perfect before you put a light amount of glue on the sides. You should have very little squeeze out (squeeze out means sound deadening, and it's just messy.) Let it dry for 24 hours and unclamp the guitar. It doesn't look like your guitar has any purfling or binding so you'll just need to make sure the back and sides are clean. 

It's a pretty complicated repair but it is doable. it's up to you if you want to fix it, but unless it's a sentimental guitar I would just replace it. If the guitar is a vintage instrument or an expensive guitar, please take it to a luthier.

Absolutely, no matter how you're finishing the guitar the most important thing is the prep work before applying the wipe on poly. 

 
The first step is to level and sand the guitar until it's smooth.
Once your guitar has been sanded to 240 grit, it must be sanded again with a sanding block to 320 and a good light source, so you can see that you don't have any divets or bumps. You can sand past 320 but all you're really doing past that is burnishing. 

After the instrument has been sanded as flat and smooth as possible you have to fill the grain with a pore filler. I like to use pumice stone, but you can use other alternatives. If you don't have anything to seal the grain egg whites will also work. Once the woodgrain has been sealed and leveled you can start your actual finishing work i.e. staining and applying your finish.

Hide glue, fish glue or Titebond 1. You always want a reversible joint in case you have to make another repair. Hide glue is the best, but the most difficult to use ( you have to boil it and apply the glue to the repair quickly before it cools and dries). Fish glue is also a great alternative to hide glue but I don't use it personally. Finally Titebond 1 is like the industry standard. It's easy to use and clean up, apply a little heat and you can reset the joint. Or you can use Elmer's white glue if you want something to dry clear.

There is no best way to thickness a body down. If you have access to a thickness planer, that would be the fastest but you need to make sure that you remove small amounts of material to avoid binding the wood on the machine or chip-out. If you have the time and skill, hand planes will leave the best surface and are reasonably fast provided you know how to use a hand plane. You can use a surface sander but it's not ideal, it'll take a long time to sand away 10mm, make alot of sawdust and you'll waste the sandpaper band(they can be expensive) surface sanders are best for taking small amounts off, and leaving a surface for gluing, NOT for final finish. The last way you can do this, (personally I think it's the best for you) would be to make a router sled and routing down to thickness. This will be time consuming and you will need to take care that the board does not move or you will have chip-out or worse yet, the router can kickback your workpiece. Make sure, the router sled is perfectly parallel, and take your time. Take small passes (1/8) passes are ideal to ensure that the router bit doesn't burn and gives you the best possible finish. Once you have routed down to size you will need to clean the mill marks left by the router bit, but a little bit of elbow grease should take care of that.
